opus-5.5.text:
I think it's important to separate two questions. One is whether AI can do the individual tasks that researchers do, and the other is whether it can do the whole job end to end. On the first, I'm genuinely amazed by how fast things are moving. A couple of years ago, if you'd told me a model could take an open problem in convex optimization, read the relevant literature, and come back with a correct, non-trivial improvement on a known bound, I would have been skeptical. Now we're seeing things like that happen. Not every day, and not on the deepest problems, but it's happening.

So, in terms of raw capability on well-posed problems, I think within the next year or two we'll see models that are as good as a strong PhD student, maybe a strong postdoc, at many of the technical pieces of research: proving lemmas, running experiments, writing code, finding connections across papers that a human would take weeks to dig up.

But "essentially everything" is a much bigger claim. A lot of what a researcher does isn't solving a problem someone handed them. It's deciding which problem matters. It's having taste, sitting with confusion for months, noticing that something weird in an experiment is actually the interesting thing. It's knowing when to abandon a direction. Those long-horizon, open-ended judgments are where I think the models are still clearly behind, and I'm honestly uncertain how quickly that gap closes. It could be faster than people expect, because every time we've said "AI can't do X," X has tended to fall. But I wouldn't bet that it's fully closed in one or two years.

What I'm confident about is that the way research is done is going to change dramatically in that timeframe. I already think of these models as collaborators. The researcher's role shifts toward asking the right questions, directing the effort, and verifying the results, while the model does more and more of the heavy lifting. That alone will accelerate science enormously, even before we reach full autonomy. And for me, that's the most exciting part: not replacing scientists, but giving every scientist a tireless, extremely knowledgeable partner.

r001.rationale: The response describes strong performance on technical research tasks, but does not say models could tackle problems requiring years of thought; it says long-horizon judgments remain behind.

r002.rationale: The response does not report that internal AI agents found errors in research papers.

r003.rationale: The response says choosing important problems is a human researcher’s role; it does not say AI generates questions humans see as potential paper foundations.

r004.rationale: The response says it would not bet that AI’s remaining gap is fully closed in one or two years, despite expecting strong performance on many technical tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those questions where you have to be careful about what you mean by "everything." If you mean the full job of a researcher, from picking the problem, to running the experiments, to writing it up, to arguing with reviewers, I'd say that's not a one-to-two-year thing. But if you decompose research into its pieces, the picture changes a lot.

Take the mathematical side, which is where I spend a lot of my time. A year ago, if you gave a model a serious open-ish problem, something at the level of a hard conjecture in convex optimization or a bound that an expert would spend a week on, it would mostly produce plausible-looking nonsense. Today, I regularly see models produce the kind of proof that I would be happy to see from a strong postdoc. Not always, and you still have to check it, but the hit rate has gone from essentially zero to something meaningful. And the slope of that curve matters more than where we are right now.

So my honest assessment is: within a year or two, I expect the models to do most of the "execution" of research. Here's a lemma, prove it. Here's a hypothesis, design and run the experiment, analyze the results. Here's a messy paper, find the gap. I think that layer gets largely automated, and that's already a huge deal, because that's where most of the hours go.

What I'm much less sure about is the taste part. Knowing which question is worth asking. Knowing that this result is interesting and that one, which looks similar, is boring. That's not obviously a capability that falls out of scaling alone, because you don't get a clean reward signal for it. Although I'll admit I've been wrong before about what falls out of scaling, so I hold that view loosely.

The other thing I'd say is that the limiting factor might not be the model at all. It might be us. Verifying a hundred proofs a day is itself a bottleneck. Deciding what to trust is a bottleneck. So even if the raw capability arrives, the actual transformation of how research gets done could lag by a few years, just because institutions and people adapt slowly.

So, short version: execution, yes, I think we're close. Judgment, I'm genuinely uncertain. And I'd rather be the person who's surprised on the upside than the one who keeps saying it can't happen.

r001.rationale: The response predicts near-term automation of research execution and discusses week-level problems, but it does not suggest models could tackle problems requiring years of thought.

r002.rationale: It says models may find gaps in papers, but does not report that internal AI agents identified errors in research papers.

r003.rationale: The response says AI’s ability to choose worthwhile questions is uncertain; it does not state that models generate research questions humans consider potential paper foundations.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says completing the full researcher job is not a one-to-two-year prospect, while expressing confidence only about automating much of research execution.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to take that possibility seriously, but I would be careful about saying “essentially everything” within a year or two. Research isn’t just answering a difficult question. It’s deciding which question matters, finding a useful way to approach it, and recognizing when a result actually changes our understanding.

You could have a system that is extraordinarily good at solving problems and still needs a human to set the direction. The next step is a system that can sustain that whole process: propose an idea, test it, discover why it fails, and come up with something better.

So I’m optimistic about the prospect, but uncertain about the timeline. What would convince me is a system repeatedly producing important discoveries with very little human guidance. That’s a much stronger demonstration than doing well on a collection of problems we already know how to evaluate.

r001.rationale: The response takes the prospect seriously but does not say models could tackle problems requiring years of thought within two years.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention internal AI agents finding errors in research papers.

r003.rationale: The response does not say AI can generate research questions that humans consider potential foundations for papers.

r004.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about the timeline and cautions against saying AI will do essentially everything researchers do within one to two years; it does not judge that it could.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to take that possibility seriously, but I would be cautious about the word “everything.” Research is a whole process: choosing a good problem, trying ideas, recognizing when something surprising matters, and deciding what to do next. Being very good at individual tasks doesn’t automatically mean you can carry that process through autonomously.

The question I would ask is: can a system take an open-ended problem, work on it for a long time, and produce a result that changes what we know, with very little human guidance? If we see that happening reliably across different fields, that would be strong evidence. Within a year or two? I wouldn’t rule it out, but I wouldn’t claim we know.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether systems can work on an open-ended problem for a long time, but does not extrapolate recent AI progress to say they could tackle problems requiring years of thought.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention internal AI agents identifying errors in research papers.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that AI models can generate research questions humans consider potential foundations for papers.

r004.rationale: The response takes the possibility seriously and says it would not rule it out, but explicitly cautions against “everything” and does not clearly judge that AI could perform more or less everything human researchers do within one to two years.
